title: Many Zionisms
hookLine: political, religious, cultural and labor Zionism, and Jews who opposed it

cards: Line up this week's stops. Jews everywhere, on every continent. Henrietta Szold, teaching newcomers.
A line at the end of the seder that faces one city. Pogroms in the Russian Empire. A broken sword in Paris.
A congress in Basel. By now it can sound as if everyone agreed on one answer. They didn't.
Seat the Jews of that time around one table and you would hear plan after plan, and some people at the table saying the whole idea was a mistake.

teach.b: Zionism, the movement for a Jewish home in the land of Israel, was never one thing.
Political Zionists, like Herzl, wanted a charter first: recognition from the great powers, then settlement. Others said, don't wait for permission, go and plant.
Cultural Zionists, led by a writer who called himself Ahad Ha'am, one of the people, wanted something smaller and deeper: a center for Hebrew culture that would renew Jewish life everywhere.

He also warned his readers that the land was not empty, that Arab villages and farmers were already there. Labor Zionists said renewal would come through work with the hands, farming and building together.
Religious Zionists, in a movement called Mizrachi, joined as observant Jews, and some of them saw God's hand in it.
And there were Jews who said no. Some Orthodox rabbis taught that the return would come with the Messiah, in God's time, and pointed to a passage in the Talmud about oaths not to force the end.
Some Reform leaders said Judaism was a faith, not a nation, and their home was the country they lived in. Jewish socialists in Eastern Europe said: stay, and fight for rights right here.
These arguments have not ended; Jews still hold all kinds of views.
The Talmud tells of a voice from heaven about two schools that disagreed: these and these are the words of the living God. The law still followed one school, but both were kept.
The tradition is used to a table full of argument.

how: Jews today hold a wide range of views on Zionism and the State of Israel, from religious and secular Zionists to Jews who oppose Zionism on religious or political grounds, and the debate is part of Jewish communal life.

games.q: you are an Orthodox rabbi hearing about the congress in Basel. what does your tradition's teaching about the end of days lead you to say?
o: wait for the Messiah, in God's time.
the rabbis split; both answers were given.
games.why: some Orthodox rabbis opposed it as forcing the end; others joined, in the religious Zionist movement Mizrachi.

practice: Bring to mind one question where you hold a strong view, and picture someone you respect who sees it differently.
Without arguing back, try saying their view in your head the way they would say it, at its best, and notice what they care about that you care about too.
You don't have to change your mind; just let the other voice finish its sentence.

wordCard.voice: Many Zionisms. Political, practical, cultural, labor and religious, each with its own plan, and beside them, Jews who opposed the idea. Today's word.

orig.note: Zionism in modern Hebrew, from Zion, a name for Jerusalem.
